items.item: A matrix that's actually measured, even by a stand-in engine, tells you something a matrix assembled from four vendors' marketing claims never can: whether the rows are even comparable.

items.item: The honest prediction isn't that a join gets uniformly cheaper or uniformly pricier as history grows — it's that the engine best at the join changes underneath the question.

items.item: Three engines solving the same last-value problem with three different names for the same idea — a cache, a sparse index, a tiered file layout — is a sign the shortcut is load-bearing, not cosmetic.

at.step: Reveal: three high-rate engines, each with its own shortcut

items.item: A join to business data isn't a TSDB feature gap to work around — it's the one row of the matrix a table format over object storage was built to win.

at.step: Reveal: the join is the lakehouse’s own case to make

items.item: Pricing two retention windows at the identical per-GB rate and still getting two different monthly numbers is what makes a capacity chain a forecast instead of a guess.

at.step: Reveal: a capacity-and-cost chain, priced at a dated unit cost

items.item: A tiering boundary doesn't fail loudly — it fails as a point that silently exists twice, or a point that silently never leaves the tier it landed in first.

at.step: Reveal: tiering duplicates points, and a late reading can miss a tier

items.item: There's no single best time-series engine, only a best engine for a named access path at a named retention — the matrix is the answer, not any one row of it.

at.step: Recap

items.item: Naming which specific access path and retention window a workload needs is what turns 'which engine should we use' from an opinion into a row lookup.
